opus-5.5.text:
So the basic idea of the lifetime anchor is this: a human goes from roughly nothing to a pretty capable general intelligence over about the first couple of decades of life. If you estimate the computation the brain does over that period, you get somewhere around 10^24 FLOP, give or take a few orders of magnitude depending on your assumptions. That's not an absurd amount of compute. It's in the range of what we already spend on frontier training runs, and we'll blow well past it soon.

I want to be careful about how much weight I put on it. I don't think it's a great anchor taken literally. Human learning is really sample-efficient in ways current ML isn't, and evolution did a lot of work setting up the brain's architecture and priors. That's arguably the expensive part, which is why people also talk about evolution anchors that come out vastly higher. So you can't just say "we have 10^24 FLOP, therefore AGI."

The reason I still find it somewhat compelling is more of an existence proof plus a bound on how inefficient we're allowed to be. It tells you that a learning algorithm exists which gets to general intelligence with that amount of compute and a modest amount of data. We're spending maybe several orders of magnitude more than that now, and compute keeps scaling. So the question becomes: is our algorithm worse than the brain's by more than a few orders of magnitude, and will we close the gap? Algorithmic progress has been pretty fast, something like several-fold efficiency gains per year on many tasks. And once AI starts meaningfully speeding up AI research, you'd expect that gap to close even faster.

So I'd put it this way. If the lifetime anchor had come out at 10^35 FLOP, I'd feel a lot more relaxed about timelines. The fact that it lands roughly where we are now, or a bit below, means I can't rule out that we're close. It's one piece of evidence among several. The more important pieces for me are the empirical trends in capabilities, like how quickly models are getting better at long-horizon agentic tasks and software engineering. But the lifetime anchor makes those trends less surprising and makes it hard to tell a story where we need some enormous unreachable amount of compute.

r001.rationale: The response says human learning is more sample-efficient than current ML and that evolution helped build the brain’s architecture and priors, so artificial systems may need several orders of magnitude more compute.

r002.rationale: It estimates human lifetime learning at about 10^24 FLOP and treats the fact that this is near or below current frontier training compute as evidence that the anchor is relevant.

r003.rationale: It says current spending is several orders of magnitude above the lifetime estimate and asks whether the algorithmic gap is larger than a few orders of magnitude, suggesting that additional orders may suffice.

r004.rationale: It notes that compute keeps scaling and says current compute will soon exceed the estimate, but does not connect the growth rate to a short time for traversing the additional orders of magnitude needed to surpass human capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
So the lifetime anchor is basically the observation that a human goes from being a baby to being a competent adult with roughly, I don't know, something like 10^24 to 10^25 FLOP of computation happening in their brain over that period, depending on how you count. That's the total compute spent on "training" a human, in the loose sense. And the thing that's striking is that the training runs we're already doing are in that ballpark. The frontier models are being trained with on the order of 10^26 FLOP, and that number is going up fast.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think the lifetime anchor is a slam dunk. There are obvious disanalogies. Humans come in with an enormous amount of prior baked in by evolution, so the lifetime compute isn't the whole story. You could argue you need to count some of the evolutionary compute too, and then you get much bigger numbers. And human learning is probably much more sample efficient than current gradient descent, so maybe we need way more compute to get the same thing.

But the reason I still put real weight on it is that it's one of the few reference points we actually have for "how much compute does it take to produce a general intelligence," and it's within a couple orders of magnitude of what we're already doing. That's a very different situation from, say, 2015, where you'd look at this and say we're like ten orders of magnitude short. When you're a couple orders of magnitude short and compute is scaling by roughly 4x to 5x per year, plus algorithmic progress on top of that, the gap closes within a few years, not decades.

The other thing is that it's not just an abstract argument anymore. We can look at what the models actually do at current compute levels, and they're doing a lot of things that look like substantial chunks of what a human does. So the anchor isn't sitting out there in isolation. It's consistent with what we're observing. If we were at 10^26 FLOP and the models were totally useless, I'd say, okay, the anchor's probably just wrong, the disanalogies dominate. But that's not what we see.

So I'd describe it as: it's one input among several, I'd put maybe moderate weight on it, but it's an input that points pretty clearly in the direction of "this could happen soon," and it's hard to construct a version of it that points toward "this is 50 years away." Even if you think current algorithms are 100x or 1000x less efficient than the brain, you're talking about a few more years of scaling, not a fundamentally different regime.

r001.rationale: The response says human learning may be more sample efficient than current gradient descent, so AI may need substantially more compute to reach comparable capabilities; it gives 100x–1000x as examples.

r002.rationale: It says current models show substantial chunks of human abilities at compute in the lifetime-compute ballpark, but does not describe roughly human-level capabilities emerging there.

r003.rationale: It mentions 100x–1000x inefficiency and a few more years of scaling, but does not clearly say that this additional compute would produce AI surpassing human capabilities.

r004.rationale: It connects compute scaling of roughly 4x–5x per year to a couple-orders-of-magnitude gap closing within a few years rather than decades.

astra-6.text:
The basic intuition is that a human gets to a pretty impressive level of general capability with the computation their brain does over a single lifetime. So that gives us one reference point for how much computation might be needed to train a powerful AI system. And if you estimate that amount of computation, it seems plausible that AI training runs could reach it relatively soon.

The big caveat is that humans don’t learn from scratch. Evolution has supplied a lot of useful structure, and you might think that producing that structure is where most of the computational difficulty lies. So I don’t think the lifetime anchor is a decisive argument.

But I also don’t think we should assume we have to recapitulate all of evolution. We’re designing learning algorithms, and we already have evidence that fairly general algorithms can acquire a wide range of capabilities. That makes me put some weight on the possibility that the relevant training requirement is closer to a human lifetime than to the entire evolutionary process. And even if that’s only one plausible possibility, it’s a reason to take short timelines seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says human lifetime brain computation is a reference point, but does not say early artificial algorithms are less computationally efficient than biology or that AI might surpass humans only above that compute level.

r002.rationale: It treats lifetime brain compute as a plausible reference for training requirements, but does not identify human-level AI emerging near that estimate as evidence.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that several additional orders of magnitude of training compute may suffice for AI to surpass human capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says AI training runs could reach the lifetime-compute reference point relatively soon, but does not connect rapid growth in training compute to traversing additional orders of magnitude toward surpassing human capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic intuition is that a human manages to become pretty capable with the amount of computation their brain does over a lifetime. So that gives us some evidence about how much computation you might need to train an AI to do the same sorts of things. And we’re getting to the point where running that amount of computation is feasible, at least under some estimates of how much computation the brain is doing.

The big objection is that humans aren’t learning from scratch. Evolution did a huge amount of work to produce a brain with useful structure and learning algorithms. So you can’t just assume that if you take a generic neural network and give it a human lifetime’s worth of computation, you’ll get a human.

But I also don’t think you should assume we have to recapitulate all of evolution. We’re designing the system, we can learn from what works in brains, and our training setup can be much more efficient in various ways. So I put some weight on the possibility that the amount of training computation required is around that lifetime scale. It’s not a decisive argument, but it gives you a plausible route to powerful AI relatively soon, and I don’t think we have strong enough reasons to rule that route out.

r001.rationale: The response raises evolution as an objection but does not say early artificial algorithms are less computationally efficient than biology or that surpassing humans would require compute above the lifetime brain-compute estimate.

r002.rationale: It says human lifetime brain computation offers evidence about the training compute needed for similar capabilities, and that training at roughly that scale is plausible.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention several additional orders of magnitude of training compute or say that this would suffice to surpass human capabilities.

r004.rationale: It suggests powerful AI could arrive relatively soon, but does not connect rapid training-compute growth to traversing additional orders of magnitude.
